note: HAND-CURATED. Not generated by any script, and deliberately not merged into substances.json - that file is regenerated from PsychonautWiki and would overwrite this. Every clinical claim below carries a source; see EVIDENCE.md for the standard. Edit by hand, and re-check the prevalence figures before trusting them: the composition of the supply moved substantially between 2024 and 2026, and stale prevalence copy is the most likely way this file goes wrong.

substances.name: Xylazine
substances.summary: A veterinary sedative, not an opioid. It is almost always found mixed into fentanyl rather than sold on its own.

whyInSupply.text: Added deliberately. Sources document two motives and do not agree on which dominates: to extend or change the effect of fentanyl, and to add weight cheaply. Some people seek it out to lengthen a short fentanyl high; others describe it as something they did not want in their supply.

sources.name: CDC — What you should know about xylazine

naloxone.lead: Naloxone does not reverse xylazine — give it anyway.
naloxone.text: Xylazine is not an opioid, so naloxone does nothing to it. But it is nearly always mixed with fentanyl, and naloxone reverses that. CDC guidance is to give naloxone in any suspected overdose. Expect the person to stay sedated after naloxone works: that is the xylazine, not a failed dose, and it is not a reason to keep giving more.

sources.name: CDC — What you should know about xylazine

overdose.title: Rescue breathing matters more here
overdose.body: Xylazine slows breathing on its own, and CDC specifically notes rescue breaths are especially helpful after xylazine. Tilt the head back, pinch the nose, give two slow breaths, then one breath every five seconds.

overdose.title: Recovery position, and stay
overdose.body: Roll the person onto their side so they do not choke if they vomit. Sedation can outlast the naloxone, so staying with them matters more than usual.

effects.title: Wounds — and what they actually are
effects.body: Xylazine is associated with severe skin wounds. They are not caused by a flesh-eating infection, whatever the news calls it: the leading explanation is that blood vessels constrict and tissue is starved of blood. Health officials say the cause is still not well understood. Wounds can appear anywhere on the body, away from any injection site, and regardless of whether someone injects, smokes, or snorts.

sources.name: Philadelphia DPH — Caring for people with xylazine-associated wounds

effects.title: Basic wound care you can do yourself
effects.body: Clean with saline, or soap and water. Apply a petroleum-based ointment and keep the wound bed moist — dry wounds do not heal. Cover with a two-layer dressing. Do not use alcohol or peroxide: they kill human cells and dry the wound out.

effects.title: When a wound needs a clinician
effects.body: Exposed bone or tendon, not being able to move a joint, fever, unexplained nausea or vomiting, confusion, pus, swelling, a smell that remains after cleaning, increasing pain, redness or warmth. Using drugs is not a reason to be refused wound care, and health departments say so explicitly.

withdrawal.text: Clinicians think a xylazine withdrawal exists. Health department guidance does not define one yet. A 2025 study of 71 patients found no measurable difference in withdrawal scores between people whose tests showed xylazine and people with fentanyl alone.

detection.text: Xylazine test strips exist and are widely given out free. They miss a lot. In one Los Angeles study of 333 fentanyl-positive samples the strips caught under half of the xylazine that was actually there, with misses concentrated in samples containing small amounts. Lidocaine can produce a false positive. A negative strip does not mean there is no xylazine.

sources.name: Test strip field performance, Los Angeles

prevalence.text: Regional, and changing fast. Across 32 jurisdictions in 2021–22, xylazine showed up in 9% of deaths involving illegally made fentanyl. That ranged from about 28% in Maryland down to roughly 1% across the whole West. It is also falling where it was most common. Philadelphia drug checking found xylazine in 97% of fentanyl samples in early 2024, and 21% by late 2025. Medetomidine replaced it. Testing for xylazine is inconsistent between jurisdictions, so counts understate it.

sources.name: CDC MMWR — Xylazine in IMF-involved deaths

substances.name: Medetomidine
substances.summary: Another veterinary sedative from the same family as xylazine, but far stronger and longer-lasting. It has largely replaced xylazine in some cities.

whyInSupply.text: Found mixed into illegally made fentanyl. Where it comes from is not established — researchers list diverted veterinary product, diverted human hospital sedative, and illicit synthesis as possibilities without settling between them. No source establishes a motive, so this page does not offer one.

naloxone.lead: Naloxone does not reverse medetomidine — give it anyway, and check breathing first.
naloxone.text: Medetomidine is not an opioid. Naloxone will have no effect on medetomidine, but it will have an effect on the fentanyl it is mixed with. Health departments have changed the order of the steps because of medetomidine: check whether the person is BREATHING before checking whether they respond to you. Someone can be breathing adequately and still be completely unresponsive from medetomidine, and checking responsiveness first may mislead you into thinking naloxone has not worked.

sources.name: PA Department of Health HAN #794 (relaying Philadelphia DPH)

overdose.title: Smaller naloxone doses are preferred
overdose.body: State guidance now prefers low-dose naloxone here — enough to restore breathing, no more. Large doses can throw someone into the severe withdrawal described below, which is itself dangerous.

overdose.title: Expect sedation to last a long time
overdose.body: Medetomidine outlasts both naloxone and xylazine. If the person is lying down, put them in the recovery position. If they are sitting, tilt their head back and to the side so their airway stays open. Check nothing is trapping their arms or legs. Stay with them until they come to.

effects.title: It does not appear to cause wounds
effects.body: Worth saying plainly, because people reasonably assume it behaves like xylazine. Health officials state medetomidine has not been shown to cause wounds, and Philadelphia saw wound-related presentations fall by roughly half after medetomidine entered its supply.

effects.title: How much stronger than xylazine
effects.body: Sources disagree. Health departments say 100–200 times; a 2026 research paper says 200–300 times. Both trace back to the same 1988 pharmacology study. What they agree on is that it is far stronger and lasts longer.

withdrawal.text: This is well documented and it is dangerous. Of 165 people hospitalized in Philadelphia between September 2024 and January 2025, 91% needed intensive care and 24% needed a breathing tube. It presents as a racing heart and very high blood pressure, sweating, tremor, nausea, restlessness, and alertness that comes and goes. It resists the usual treatments — opioids, benzodiazepines and clonidine — and most people responded to dexmedetomidine instead. It can begin within hours of last use and peaks around 18 to 36 hours. It can be triggered by receiving naloxone. If you are withdrawing and your heart is racing and your blood pressure is high, this is a reason to get to a hospital.

detection.text: They have one quirk. The drug comes in two mirror-image forms, and some strip lots only react to one of them. So a negative can be wrong, depending on which form is in there and which lot you have.

prevalence.text: Heavily concentrated in the Northeast and close to absent in the West. CDC drug-checking across 20 sites in late 2025 found medetomidine in about 74% of opioid-positive samples in the Northeast, 56% in the Midwest, 30% in the South, and under 4% in the West. In Philadelphia it went from absent in early 2024 to 88% of fentanyl samples by late 2025. Where you are matters more for this substance than for almost anything else on this app.

substances.nameNote: Dexmedetomidine is not another name for this. It is the mirror-image form, sold as Precedex, and it is a licensed hospital sedative — one of the things used to treat medetomidine withdrawal. Street samples tested so far have all been the racemic form.

substances.name: Nitazenes
substances.summary: A family of synthetic opioids never approved for medical use anywhere. Unlike xylazine and medetomidine, these ARE opioids — so naloxone works on them.

whyInSupply.text: Sold as opioids in their own right and also found mixed into other drugs. They were first made about sixty years ago as candidate painkillers and were never approved. Why they appear where they do is not well characterized, and this page does not guess.

naloxone.lead: Naloxone works on nitazenes at normal doses.
naloxone.text: You may have read that nitazenes need many times the usual amount of naloxone. The published evidence does not support that. A 2025 review found a median effective dose of about 1.2 mg, and under 1 mg when given before reaching hospital — ordinary doses. Some people need a second dose, as with any strong opioid. The genuine difference is duration: the nitazene can outlast the naloxone, so someone can wake up and then go back under. Stay with them, and call 911 even if they seem fine.

overdose.title: Do not leave after they wake up
overdose.body: The most important difference with nitazenes is how long they last. In one review, some cases needed naloxone kept running continuously because the opioid effect persisted. Naloxone wearing off before the drug does is the specific thing to watch for: breathing can stop again after everyone in the room has relaxed. Stay with them.

effects.title: On strength claims
effects.body: "Hundreds of times stronger than fentanyl" is true of some members of this family in laboratory tests and not true of the family as a whole — CDC notes metonitazene's potency is similar to fentanyl's. Researchers also note that real-world potency often comes out lower than lab figures, and that human data is scarce.

detection.text: Nitazene strips have been sold since early 2024. A laboratory evaluation found they picked up 24 of 33 nitazenes tested, and needed a fairly large amount present to react. The consistent blind spot is a related group called desnitazenes, which the strips are not built to catch. The researchers put it plainly: a negative result does not mean a sample is safe. The strips also cannot tell you which nitazene it is or how much.

prevalence.text: Rising, and still numerically small. Tennessee recorded no nitazene-involved deaths in 2019, 10 in 2020 and 42 in 2021. Nationally, confirmed nitazene-involved deaths number in the hundreds per year against roughly 80,000 overdose deaths overall in 2024. Two things are true at once: this is a small share of deaths, and it is genuinely undercounted, because few laboratories test for nitazenes at all. Mid-Atlantic drug checking found none at all in late 2025.

substances.name: BTMPS
substances.summary: An industrial chemical used to stop plastic degrading in sunlight. It is not a drug, has never been studied in people, and began appearing in the fentanyl supply in 2024.

whyInSupply.text: Nobody knows. Researchers offer two possibilities — a change in how fentanyl is being made, or simple dilution — and explicitly decline to choose between them. Samples containing BTMPS did have less fentanyl in them, which fits the dilution idea without proving it.

naloxone.lead: Unknown — respond as you would to any opioid overdose.
naloxone.text: It turns up alongside fentanyl, so the guidance is the standard one. Give naloxone. Give rescue breaths between doses if they are not breathing. Stop once they breathe on their own. Put them on their side if they stay sedated. Call 911.

effects.title: There is no human research at all
effects.body: Health officials state there are no studies of BTMPS use in people. What exists is animal data showing heart toxicity and eye damage. People who have encountered it report ringing ears, blurred vision and a taste like plastic or bug spray when smoking it, and burning when injecting — these are self-reports, not clinical findings.

detection.text: There is no test strip for BTMPS. Finding it requires laboratory equipment, which in practice means a drug-checking service rather than anything you can do yourself.

prevalence.text: Uncertain, and falling where it was measured. A study across nine US locations in 2024 found BTMPS in about a third of drug samples from Los Angeles and Philadelphia. Philadelphia's health department published its own figures of 16% and 11% in June and July 2024, with the explicit caveat that too few samples were tested to know how widespread it is. In the Mid-Atlantic it peaked at 46% of fentanyl samples in late 2024 and had fallen to 4% a year later.

substances.name: Tusi
substances.soldAs: Sold under its own name — for something it is not
substances.summary: A pink powder sold under a drug's name that is not the drug. It is almost always a ketamine blend, usually with MDMA, and it very rarely contains either 2C-B — the substance the name comes from — or cocaine.

whyInSupply.text: The pink color is branding, not an ingredient. It tells you nothing about what is inside. Each batch is mixed by hand, so two bags of the same pink powder can hold different drugs in different amounts.

sources.name: When pink powders shift the drug landscape (Int J Drug Policy, 2025)

naloxone.lead: Naloxone does not reverse ketamine — give naloxone anyway.
naloxone.text: Give it anyway if their breathing is bad, or if you cannot rule out opioids. Opioids have been found in some pink powders. You cannot tell by looking. And naloxone does nothing at all to a person with no opioids in them.

sources.name: Poison Control — What is pink cocaine?

overdose.title: On their side, before anything else
overdose.body: The most likely way this kills somebody is not breathing failure — it is choking on vomit while too far under to roll over. Ketamine makes people vomit and takes away the ability to move. Put them on their side and leave them there.

sources.name: Poison Control — What is pink cocaine?

overdose.title: Being unable to move is not the same as being asleep
overdose.body: At a high enough dose ketamine leaves somebody awake, aware and unable to respond or call for help. Somebody who has stopped answering has not necessarily stopped hearing. Stay with them, say what you are doing, and do not leave them alone to sleep it off.

sources.name: Poison Control — What is pink cocaine?

overdose.title: Overheating, from the half you did not plan for
overdose.body: Most pink powder carries MDMA as well, which pushes body temperature and heart rate up. Somebody hot, confused and not making sense needs cooling and an ambulance, and that is a different emergency from the sedation above — both can be present in one person at once.

sources.name: What Is Pink Cocaine? (J Med Chem, 2025)

effects.title: The ratio is the danger, not the pairing
effects.body: Ketamine and MDMA taken together deliberately are not an especially risky pair, and the combination checker on this app says so. That rating assumes you chose both and know how much of each you took. In a pink powder you know neither: measured samples have run from roughly 40% to 90% ketamine by weight, with MDMA anywhere from 10% to 45%. The same measured line off two different bags can be two very different doses of two different drugs.

sources.name: When pink powders shift the drug landscape (Int J Drug Policy, 2025)

effects.title: The stimulant hides how far under you are going
effects.body: MDMA is a stimulant and ketamine is a sedative, and somebody feeling the first can keep taking more of a powder that is mostly the second. The sedation arrives later and all at once. This is the mechanism behind most of the reported harm, rather than any single ingredient being unusually potent.

sources.name: What Is Pink Cocaine? (J Med Chem, 2025)

detection.text: Reagents do not help either. A reagent reacts to whatever there is most of. So a pink powder that is 80% ketamine reads as ketamine, whatever else is in it. And it cannot tell you the proportions, which is the part that varies.

prevalence.text: Consistent across every dataset that has looked. The DEA examined 960 pink powders seized since 2020 and found 2C-B in four of them; an analysis of nearly a thousand DEA seizures found 99.5% were ketamine mixed with something else. Of 68 samples submitted to DrugsData between 2016 and 2024 as “pink cocaine”, “tusi” or “2C-B”, 94% contained ketamine and 81% MDMA. In Spain, 470 tusi samples ran 93.2% ketamine and 92.1% MDMA against 3.6% 2C-B. A 2025 Miami-Dade medical examiner series of fourteen powders taken from eight deaths found 2C-B in none of them.
